entries.title: Hindi at a glance
body: Hindi is an Indo-Aryan language written in Devanagari. The verb comes last (subject, object, verb), and where English has prepositions Hindi has postpositions after the noun.

Every noun is masculine or feminine, and verbs and adjectives agree with it. Spoken Hindi and Urdu are largely mutually intelligible; Urdu is written in a Perso-Arabic script and draws more vocabulary from Persian and Arabic.

examples.e: I drink tea. (said by a man)

entries.title: How Devanagari works
body: Each consonant letter carries a built-in short a: क is ka. Other vowels are written with marks (mātrā) attached to the consonant; a separate vowel letter is used only at the start of a word or after another vowel.
A line along the top (śirorekhā) joins the letters of a word. The virāma ् removes the built-in vowel, and two consonants with no vowel between them often merge into a conjunct.

examples.t: क् + ष = क्ष · त् + र = त्र · ज् + ञ = ज्ञ
examples.e: three conjuncts with their own shapes

entries.title: Nasal marks: anusvāra and candrabindu
entries.body: A dot above (ं, anusvāra) stands for an n or m sound that matches the next consonant, or nasalizes a vowel. The moon and dot (ँ, candrabindu) nasalizes the vowel, as in French. Many writers use the plain dot for both, especially where a vowel mark already sits on top.

examples.e: Hindi: the dot and the half-न are two spellings of the same sound
I (dot used because ै already sits on top)

entries.title: Aspirated and retroflex consonants
body: Hindi distinguishes plain and aspirated consonants: क ka and ख kha are different letters and change meaning. The h in transliteration is a puff of air, not a separate sound.
It also has two kinds of t and d. {Dental} त थ द ध are made with the tongue on the teeth; {retroflex} ट ठ ड ढ with the tongue tip curled back. English t and d sound retroflex to Hindi ears.

entries.title: Silent a: schwa deletion
entries.body: The built-in a is usually not said at the end of a word, and often dropped in the middle of a word when a long vowel follows. Read by the letters and you'd say too many syllables.

entries.title: Postpositions
entries.body: Little words that mean in, on, from and to come after the noun. A noun before a postposition takes its oblique form.

entries.title: का, की, के agree with the thing owned
entries.body: The possessive changes to match the noun that follows it, not the owner. Use का before a masculine singular noun, की before any feminine noun, and के before a masculine plural or oblique noun. My, your and our work the same way: मेरा, मेरी, मेरे.

entries.title: The oblique form
entries.body: Before a postposition, masculine nouns ending in -ā change to -e in the singular, and all plurals end in -on. Other nouns change only in the plural.

entries.title: Pronouns and होना (to be)
entries.body: Hindi has three levels of you. {आप} is polite and the safe default with adults; {तुम} is for friends and people younger than you; {तू} is very intimate or rude. Third-person वे / ये are also used for one person, as a mark of respect.

entries.title: Present habitual: बोलता हूँ
entries.body: Take the verb stem (drop -nā), add -tā / -tī / -te for the subject's gender and number, then the right form of होना.

entries.title: Present progressive: खा रहा हूँ
entries.body: For an action happening now, use the stem + रहा / रही / रहे + होना.

entries.title: The past tense and ने
body: In the simple past, transitive verbs (ones that take an object) mark their subject with {ने}, and the verb then agrees with the object instead of the subject.
Intransitive verbs like go and come don't use ने and agree with the subject as usual.

examples.e: I read the book. (पढ़ी is feminine to match किताब)
She went home. (no ने: go is intransitive)

entries.title: Numbers
body: एक, दो, तीन, चार, पाँच, छह, सात, आठ, नौ, दस. Unlike most languages, every number from 1 to 100 has its own word that has to be learned; the tens and units blend irregularly.
Large numbers group in the Indian way: a lākh is 100,000 (written 1,00,000) and a karoṛ is 10 million (1,00,00,000).

examples.e: How are you? (to a man; कैसी to a woman)
